note: Rig It Right (Guide School, 2026-11-15). General inshore practice for the Ten Thousand Islands and the Everglades backcountry: the rig most guides reach for first in each set of conditions, not the only one that works. No regulations here (sizes, seasons and bag limits change; link to FWC). Book ties cite data/gear.json.

rules.when: Can’t see your lure a foot down?
rules.then: Make noise, flash or smell: a popping cork, a gold spoon, a live shrimp.
Go quiet, light and natural. Splashy rigs send fish running.
Go weedless, or you’ll catch salad on every cast.

rules.when: Deep, or the tide is ripping?
rules.then: Add weight until you can feel the bottom.
Throw something small and heavy that cuts through it.

rules.when: Dawn, dusk or a gray sky?
rules.then: Look up. Low light is topwater time.
Slow down, or go find water that is. Moving water feeds fish.

rigs.name: Popping cork
rigs.parts: A cupped cork, a foot and a half to two feet of leader, a hook or a light jig, and a live shrimp.
rigs.how: Cast it out and let it settle. Pop the rod tip twice, then wait. The pop sounds like a fish feeding, and the shrimp hangs right above the grass.
rigs.best: Grass flats two to five feet deep, moving water, stained water and a breezy chop. The easiest rig for a beginner: when the cork goes under, reel.
rigs.skip: Dead-calm, gin-clear, skinny water. The splash sends fish running.

book.line: How Matt caught his first snook, and most of his redfish.

rigs.name: Jig and paddle tail
rigs.parts: A lead jig head and a soft-plastic paddle tail. An eighth of an ounce for the shallows, a quarter ounce for depth, wind or current.
rigs.how: Cast, let it sink, then hop it or swim it back. The tail thumps the whole way.
rigs.best: Covering water when you don’t know where the fish are: sand potholes, channel edges, casting into the wind.
rigs.skip: Thick grass and oyster shell. The open hook grabs everything.

rigs.name: Free-lined live bait
rigs.parts: Leader, a small circle hook and a live shrimp or baitfish. No cork, no weight.
rigs.how: Cast up-current and let the tide carry it along the roots and under the branches, the way real food arrives.
rigs.best: Clear water and a gentle, steady current along the mangroves. The quietest rig in the box, for fish that have seen it all.
rigs.skip: Hard wind or a ripping tide: with no weight it never gets down to the fish.

book.line: Snapper tosses a small live bait into the current, and hooks the giant.

rigs.name: Knocker rig
rigs.parts: An egg sinker that slides down the leader to knock against a circle hook, baited with shrimp or cut bait.
rigs.how: Drop it straight to the bottom, keep the line tight and wait for the thump.
rigs.best: Deep holes, passes and pilings with a strong current. Bottom fish: snapper, sheepshead, black drum, grouper.
rigs.skip: Shallow grass flats. It just buries itself.

rigs.name: Weedless soft plastic
rigs.parts: A slim soft-plastic jerk shad on a wide-gap hook with a little belly weight, the hook point tucked back into the plastic.
rigs.how: Cast past the fish, never on its head. Twitch, twitch, pause.
rigs.best: Water under two feet, thick grass, oyster edges and tailing redfish. It lands softly and slides through anything.
rigs.skip: Deep water or heavy current: too light to get down.

rigs.name: Weedless gold spoon
rigs.parts: A gold spoon with one fixed hook and a wire weed guard, on a small swivel so it doesn’t twist the line.
rigs.how: Cast it a mile and reel just fast enough to feel it wobble above the grass.
rigs.best: Stained or muddy water, wind, and hunting for redfish across a big flat. Fish see the flash and feel the thump.
rigs.skip: Deep holes. It’s a shallow-water searcher.

book.line: A spoon was Matt’s first cast after the storm.

rigs.name: Topwater plug
rigs.parts: A floating cigar-shaped plug, tied on with a loop knot so it can swing.
rigs.how: Twitch the rod tip on a slack line so the plug zig-zags: ‘walking the dog.’ When a fish blows up on it, wait until you feel weight before you lift.
rigs.best: Dawn, dusk and overcast days on a calm surface, along shallow shorelines and flats. Snook and trout.
rigs.skip: Bright midday sun, a hard chop, or floating grass that fouls the hooks.

rigs.name: Big live bait, heavy leader
rigs.parts: A big circle hook, several feet of heavy leader and a live mullet or crab.
rigs.how: Set the bait ahead of rolling fish and let them find it. When one eats, don’t jerk: just come tight and hang on. When it jumps, bow the rod to it.
rigs.best: Tarpon rolling in a pass or a river mouth with the tide moving.
rigs.skip: Everything else. This is big-game tackle.

scenarios.scene: A wide grass flat. Trout are scattered over the grass and you need to call them in.
scenarios.why: The pop calls trout from across the flat, and the cork holds the shrimp just above the grass where they can find it.

scenarios.scene: A deep bend in the river with a fallen tree on the bottom. Mangrove snapper live in the branches.
scenarios.why: Only weight gets a bait to the bottom in that current. The sinker rides against the hook, so the bait stays put right by the tree.

scenarios.scene: First light. The water is a mirror, and snook are popping bait along the shoreline.
scenarios.why: Low light and a calm surface: the fish are already looking up. A plug walking across the top is one of the best bites there is.

scenarios.scene: Redfish tails are waving above the surface as they root in thick turtle grass.
scenarios.why: It lands softly and slides through the grass without snagging. A jig’s open hook would catch grass, and a cork’s splash would send those tails running.

scenarios.scene: Silver backs are rolling in the pass. Tarpon, and big ones.
scenarios.why: A fish that can weigh more than you needs a big bait, a big circle hook and a leader its sandpaper mouth can’t wear through.

scenarios.scene: Snook are tucked under the branches of a mangrove point, and the tide is sliding gently along the roots.
scenarios.why: In clear water at midday the fish can see everything. A shrimp with no cork and no weight drifts under the branches exactly the way real food does.

scenarios.scene: It has blown hard all night. The flat is the color of chocolate milk and the redfish could be anywhere on it.
scenarios.why: It casts like a bullet into the wind, and in dirty water fish find it by flash and thump. You can search the whole flat with it.

scenarios.scene: New water. You have no idea where the fish are, only that there are sandy potholes spread across a mile of bay.
scenarios.why: When you don’t know where they are, cover water. A jig casts far, sinks fast and lets you check a pothole a minute until one bites back.

scenarios.scene: Trout and jacks are holding deep along a channel edge. The wind is in your face and your light lures keep sailing over their heads.
scenarios.why: Go up to the quarter-ounce head. The extra weight punches through the wind and gets down to the fish before the current sweeps it away.

scenarios.scene: Sheepshead are nibbling barnacles off the dock pilings, right against the wood.
scenarios.why: Bottom fish on structure want a small bait held right beside the piling. Use a small hook and a piece of shrimp: sheepshead are famous bait thieves.

scenarios.scene: The falling tide is pulling bait off an oyster bar, and redfish are waiting on the edge of the shell.
scenarios.why: Oyster shell eats open hooks and cuts line. A tucked hook point crawls over the bar and drops off the edge to the fish.

scenarios.scene: A gray, still afternoon. A creek is draining a flat, and snook are blowing up on the bait washing out of it.
scenarios.why: It doesn’t have to be dawn. Under a gray sky on calm water, fish feed on top all afternoon, and they’re already doing it.

scenarios.scene: The trout are here, you can see them. But every time your popping cork lands, they scatter.
scenarios.why: The rig that calls fish in dirty water scares them in clear water. Take the cork off, go quiet, and let a bare shrimp drift to them.

scenarios.scene: Snook are holding deep against the roots. Your free-lined shrimp keeps getting swept away over their heads.
scenarios.why: Same fish, different water. When the tide rips you need weight to get down to them, so bounce a quarter-ounce jig along the bottom.

scenarios.scene: Two days of wind have turned the flat to mud. The wind has finally quit, but a fish couldn’t see a lure a foot away.
scenarios.why: When they can’t see, let them hear and smell. The cork makes the noise and the live shrimp does the rest.

scenarios.scene: Sunrise on a calm, skinny flat: perfect for a topwater plug, except the surface is covered in floating grass.
scenarios.why: A plug’s dangling hooks collect floating grass on every cast, and a fouled lure catches nothing. The right rig is the one that stays clean.

scenarios.scene: Good water, a mixed bag of trout, reds and snook. Your little cousin is aboard and has never held a rod.
scenarios.why: A guide rigs for the angler, not just the fish. Anyone can fish a cork: pop it, watch it, and reel when it goes under.

scenarios.scene: A school of redfish is pushing a wake across the flat, forty yards off and moving away. You get one cast.
scenarios.why: Nothing else in the box reaches them. The spoon flies forty yards, won’t snag, and flashes where a moving school can see it.
